subject: ophthalmology
title: Diseases of the conjunctiva

steps.tx: **Acute bacterial conjunctivitis** glues the lids with mucopurulent discharge from staphylococcal, streptococcal or Haemophilus infection in children. **Viral disease** from adenovirus waters with follicles, preauricular nodes, recent respiratory contact and high infectivity, while membranes mark severe adenoviral or streptococcal variants. Hyperacute gonococcal disease pours copious pus with corneal perforation risk in neonates and adults and needs systemic ceftriaxone with lavage. Chlamydial inclusion disease causes chronic follicular inflammation in sexually active adults and partners need azithromycin.
steps.say: Bacterial conjunctivitis is the infection that glues the lids together with yellow discharge that crusts overnight. Viral disease waters instead and it enlarges the node in front of the ear after a recent cold, so it spreads fast through hands and towels. Hyperacute gonococcal infection pours pus and it can melt the cornea within hours, so it needs urgent systemic treatment with washing. Chronic follicular disease in a sexually active adult suggests chlamydial infection and partners also need treatment.

steps.tx: **Trachoma** from Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes A to C blinds through repeated childhood infection that scars the lid inward. McCallan staging tracks follicular activity to cicatricial quiet while **WHO FISTO** grading records follicles, intense inflammation, scarring, trichiasis and corneal opacity. Diagnosis needs upper tarsal follicles with pannus, Herbert pits or stellate scarring. The SAFE strategy combines surgery for trichiasis, antibiotics with single dose azithromycin, facial cleanliness and environmental improvement. Trichiasis surgery with bilamellar tarsal rotation precedes corneal opacity.
steps.say: Trachoma blinds villages through repeated chlamydial infection that scars the upper lid and drags lashes inward. Examiners look for follicles under the upper lid with pannus creeping over the cornea and small pits called Herbert pits. The SAFE strategy combines lid surgery for inturned lashes with azithromycin for the community plus face washing and cleaner surroundings. Surgery for trichiasis comes before the cornea turns opaque, so early referral preserves sight.

vis.alt: Clinical signs of Trachoma, a blinding disease caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Features include upper tarsal follicles, pannus, Herbert pits, lid scarring, trichiasis, and corneal opacity.

steps.tx: **Allergic conjunctivitis** itches with ropy discharge and papillae in seasonal hay fever and perennial dust mite patterns. **Vernal keratoconjunctivitis** strikes atopic boys with giant cobblestone papillae, Trantas dots and shield ulcers that threaten vision. Management avoids rubbing, cools with lubricants and uses mast cell stabilisers with antihistamines, reserving short steroids or ciclosporin and supratarsal injections for shield disease. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis scars lids chronically. Contact lens overwear breeds giant papillary disease with mucus and lens intolerance, eased by lens holiday and fit change.
steps.say: Allergy itches more than any other conjunctivitis and it produces ropy discharge with raised papillae under the lid. Vernal disease affects atopic boys and it builds giant cobblestone papillae with white Trantas dots and a shield ulcer that threatens vision. Treatment starts with no rubbing plus cool lubricants, antihistamines and mast cell stabilisers, while shield ulcers need steroids or ciclosporin under supervision. Overworn contact lenses also grow giant papillae with mucus, so a lens holiday restores tolerance.

steps.tx: Degenerative surface disease separates by the limbus. **Pinguecula** forms a benign yellow nasal nodule that never crosses the limbus and needs only lubricants with excision for cosmetic concern. **Pterygium** spreads as a wing shaped fibrovascular growth that invades cornea under ultraviolet drive and needs excision with autograft when it encroaches on vision. Dry eye burns with fluctuating vision, low tear breakup time and punctate staining and responds to preservative free tears, punctal plugs and ciclosporin. Foamy Bitot spots flag vitamin A deficiency in malnourished children.
steps.say: A pinguecula sits as a yellow nasal nodule and it never crosses onto the cornea. A pterygium behaves like a wing of vessels and tissue that crosses the limbus and drags toward the pupil after years of sun exposure. Encroaching growth needs excision with an autograft because bare removal recurs fast. Dry eye burns with fluctuating vision and it improves with preservative free tears and punctal plugs, while foamy patches in a thin child suggest vitamin A deficiency.

steps.tx: This paired photo contrasts **pterygium** on one side with **pinguecula** on the other for the exam. Pterygium crosses the limbus as a fleshy ultraviolet driven wing with vessels, and encroaching lesions need autograft excision to limit recurrence. Pinguecula stays back as a yellow nasal nodule without corneal invasion and usually needs only reassurance with lubricants. The comparison teaches the limbus rule that separates the two lesions at a glance. Spotting the crossing edge earns easy marks.
steps.say: This paired photo places pterygium beside pinguecula for direct comparison. The pterygium wing crosses the limbus with visible vessels after chronic sun exposure, so encroaching cases need excision with an autograft. The pinguecula remains a yellow nasal nodule that stops short of the cornea and usually needs only reassurance. The limbus rule separates the pair in seconds, and examiners love this spot diagnosis.
